title: Insulin, glucagon, cortisol and GH: keeping glucose up
goal: Explain how a fall in insulin and a rise in glucagon, helped by cortisol and growth hormone, keep blood glucose steady during exercise, and how contraction lets glucose into muscle without insulin.

steps.title: Four grams to defend
steps.text:
The blood of a 70 kg adult holds only about **4–5 g of glucose** [[c:ef-four-grams]], and the brain depends on it. Working muscle pulls glucose out of the blood much faster than at rest, so in a long run that small pool would empty quickly if nothing refilled it.

The refill comes from the liver: it breaks down its glycogen and makes new glucose by [gluconeogenesis](g:gluconeogenesis). In healthy people, exercise raises the liver's glucose output ([rate of appearance](g:rate-of-appearance)) and muscle glucose use together, so blood glucose stays nearly constant [[c:ef-matching]].

The signals that keep the two matched are mostly hormones from the pancreas. When the liver's glycogen runs low late in a long event, that matching fails and blood glucose falls.

claims.text: About 4 g of glucose circulates in the blood of a 70 kg person, defended by a sophisticated control system.

evidence.quote: Four grams of glucose circulates in the blood of a person weighing 70 kg.
In accordance with the importance of these 4 g of glucose, a sophisticated control system is in place to maintain blood glucose constant.

claims.text: Exercise raises liver glucose production and glucose use together, so blood glucose stays relatively constant.

evidence.quote: Under normal healthy conditions, exercise initiates simultaneous elevations in hepatic glucose production (glucose R(a)) and glucose utilisation. As a result, circulating glucose levels are maintained at a relatively constant level.

steps.title: Insulin down, glucagon up
steps.text:
In exercise lasting more than about 20 min, [insulin](g:insulin) release falls and [glucagon](g:glucagon) rises [[c:ef-pancreas-shift]]. In prolonged running, glucagon tripled while insulin stayed low [[c:ef-galbo-glucagon]].

Both changes push the liver the same way. The rise in glucagon drives glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis; the fall in insulin is needed for liver glycogen breakdown and makes the liver more sensitive to glucagon [[c:ef-liver]]. Low insulin also lifts the brake on lipolysis, so more fat reaches the muscles.

Why does insulin fall? It means "store", the opposite of what a rider needs. How the pancreas senses exercise is unclear: cutting its nerves doesn't stop the response [[c:ef-pancreas-shift]]. Whether adrenaline takes over at very high intensity is debated (see the box).

claims.text: During sustained exercise (more than about 20 min) insulin secretion falls and glucagon, catecholamines and cortisol rise; denervating the pancreas does not stop the glucagon and insulin responses.

evidence.quote: If exercise is sustained (>~20 min), a decrease in insulin secretion and increases in glucagon, catecholamines, and cortisol secretion, among other hormones, are observed.
Surprisingly, denervation of the pancreas does not impair the glucagon and insulin responses to exercise, suggesting that an endocrine or a paracrine factor may be involved.

claims.text: During prolonged running at 76% VO₂max, glucagon rose progressively to three times its resting value, while insulin was depressed.

evidence.quote: During prolonged exercise glucagon increased progressively to three times (226 plus or minus 40) the resting value.
Insulin concentrations were depressed during work except for the heaviest load.

claims.text: The rise in glucagon and the fall in insulin are the major drivers of liver glucose output in moderate exercise; the fall in insulin is needed for liver glycogen breakdown and sensitises the liver to glucagon.

evidence.quote: The rise in glucagon is required for the full increment in hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, 32 , 33 while the fall in insulin 33 , 34 is necessary for hepatic glycogenolysis.
Finally, exercise causes a fall in insulin that sensitizes the liver to glucagon.
In large part, exercise-induced changes in the pancreatic secretion of glucagon and insulin are primarily responsible for the stimulation of glucose R(a) during moderate exercise.

debate.question: In very hard exercise (above about 80% VO₂max), do catecholamines take over control of the liver's glucose output?

sides.position: No clear sign: blocking adrenergic receptors, in the whole body (people) or only in the liver (dogs), has not reduced liver glucose output in heavy exercise; glucagon and insulin stay in charge.
Possibly: in heavy exercise and poorly controlled diabetes, sympathetic drive rises and has long been thought to add a major push on the liver.

steps.title: The glucagon-to-insulin ratio
steps.problem: During a 90 min ride, glucagon rises from 80 to 160 pg·mL⁻¹ and insulin falls from 10 to 5 µU·mL⁻¹. The liver responds to the two together, so researchers often use the glucagon ÷ insulin ratio. By what factor does the ratio change?
steps: Before: 80 ÷ 10 = 8. After: 160 ÷ 5 = 32. (The ratio has odd units; only its change matters.)
Shortcut: glucagon × 2 and insulin ÷ 2 multiply: 2 × 2 = 4. Adding them (2 + 2) gives the same answer here only by chance.

steps.title: Glucose into muscle without insulin
steps.text:
If insulin falls, how does working muscle take up *more* glucose? Contraction moves [GLUT4](g:glut4) to the fibre membrane by its own signals, such as calcium (Ca²⁺) and AMPK, an energy-sensing enzyme [[c:ef-contraction]].

In isolated rat muscle, blocking insulin's signalling pathway stopped insulin's effect on GLUT4 but left contraction's untouched; the two together added up [[c:ef-distinct]].

| | insulin | contraction |
|---|---|---|
| signal | insulin receptor | Ca²⁺, AMPK and others |
| when | after a meal | during exercise |
| GLUT4 to membrane | yes | yes, by a separate route |

So muscle can feed itself while low insulin lets the liver and fat tissue release fuel. The catch: with high insulin *and* contraction, both doors are open at once, and blood glucose can drop.

claims.text: Muscle contraction moves GLUT4 from storage depots to the membrane, through signals including AMPK, Ca²⁺ and NOS.

evidence.quote: Glucose enters the muscle cell via facilitated diffusion through the GLUT4 glucose transporter which translocates from intracellular storage depots to the plasma membrane and T-tubules upon muscle contraction.

Contraction-induced molecular signaling is complex and involves a variety of signaling molecules including AMPK, Ca(2+), and NOS in the proximal part of the signaling cascade as well as GTPases, Rab, and SNARE proteins and cytoskeletal components in the distal part.

claims.text: In rat muscle, contraction moved GLUT4 to the surface by a route distinct from insulin's, and the effects of the two added together.

evidence.quote: The results provide evidence that contraction stimulates translocation of GLUT4 in skeletal muscle through a mechanism distinct from that of insulin.
The combined effects of contraction and maximal insulin stimulation were greater than either stimulation alone on glucose transport activity

steps.title: Cortisol and growth hormone: the slower helpers
steps.text:
[Cortisol](g:cortisol), a steroid from the adrenal cortex, supports glucose supply over hours: it promotes gluconeogenesis and the breakdown of protein and fat for fuel. It needs a hard enough effort. In 12 men, 30 min at 40% VO₂max gave no rise, 60% about +40%, and 80% about +83% [[c:ef-cortisol]]. Long sessions raise it too.

[Growth hormone](g:growth-hormone), a peptide from the pituitary, raises fat breakdown. Its strongest exercise trigger seems to be at least 10 min above the lactate threshold [[c:ef-gh]].

| hormone | acts within | main fuel job |
|---|---|---|
| glucagon, low insulin | minutes | liver glucose output |
| adrenaline | seconds | muscle glycogen, fat release |
| cortisol, GH | hours | gluconeogenesis, fat use |

claims.text: Cortisol rose after 30 min at 60% and 80% VO₂max (about +40% and +83%), but not at 40%.

evidence.quote: The percent change in cortisol from pre- to post-sampling at each session was: resting-control, 40, 60, and 80% sessions (mean+/-SD) =-6.6+/-3.5%, +5.7+/-11.0%, +39.9+/-11.8%, and +83.1+/-18.5%, respectively.
Collectively, the cortisol findings support the view that moderate to high intensity exercise provokes increases in circulating cortisol levels.

claims.text: The growth hormone response to endurance exercise appears greatest with exercise above the lactate threshold for at least 10 min.

evidence.quote: An exercise intensity above lactate threshold and for a minimum of 10 minutes appears to elicit the greatest stimulus to the secretion of hGH.

points: Blood holds only about 4–5 g of glucose; in exercise the liver's output rises with muscle uptake to keep it steady.
In sustained exercise insulin falls and glucagon rises; together they are the main drivers of liver glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis.
Contraction moves GLUT4 to the membrane by its own route, so muscle takes up glucose while insulin is low.
Cortisol (from about 60% VO₂max in one small study of men, or in long sessions) and growth hormone (above the lactate threshold) support fuel supply over hours.

variants.stem: During a steady 90 min ride without food, what happens to the cyclist's blood insulin?

options.text: It falls below the resting level
options.why: Right: insulin release falls in sustained exercise, letting the liver release glucose and fat tissue release fatty acids.

options.text: It rises, to push glucose into the working muscles
options.why: A common belief. Contraction moves GLUT4 by its own route, so muscle doesn't need extra insulin; insulin falls.

options.text: It stays at the resting level throughout
options.why: Insulin doesn't hold steady: it falls within about 20 min of sustained exercise.

options.text: It rises at first, then drops to zero
options.why: Insulin falls from the start of sustained exercise, but it doesn't vanish; a low level remains.

variants.stem: A marathoner runs at a steady pace for 2 h without carbohydrate. How do her insulin and glucagon change?

options.text: Insulin falls and glucagon rises
options.why: Right: this pair of changes drives the liver to release glucose.

options.text: Insulin rises and glucagon falls
options.why: This is the after-a-meal pattern, the opposite of what sustained exercise does.

options.text: Both rise together
options.why: Insulin and glucagon pull in opposite directions; in exercise insulin falls while glucagon rises.

options.text: Both fall together
options.why: Glucagon rises during prolonged exercise; in one study it reached three times its resting value.

variants.stem: About how much glucose circulates in the blood of a 70 kg runner at rest?

options.text: About 4–5 g
options.why: Right: a tiny pool, which is why the liver must refill it continuously during exercise.

options.text: About 100 g
options.why: That is roughly the liver's glycogen store, not the glucose in the blood.

options.text: About 400 g
options.why: That is roughly the glycogen stored in all the muscles.

options.text: About 40 g
options.why: Ten times too much: blood holds only about 4–5 g, roughly a teaspoon.

variants.stem: During a moderate 1 h run, what is the main signal that drives the liver to release more glucose?

options.text: The rise in glucagon together with the fall in insulin
options.why: Right: in moderate exercise these pancreatic changes are mainly responsible for the liver's glucose output.

options.text: Adrenaline acting on the liver's β receptors
options.why: This was assumed for decades, but blocking adrenergic receptors hasn't reduced liver glucose output.

options.text: Cortisol switching on liver genes
options.why: Cortisol helps over hours, but its rise is too slow and too small at moderate intensity to drive minute-to-minute output.

options.text: A fall in blood glucose acting alone
options.why: Blood glucose barely falls in moderate exercise; the liver output rises through the pancreatic hormones.

variants.stem: During a 2 h ride, a cyclist's glucagon rises from 90 to 135 pg·mL⁻¹ and insulin falls from 12 to 6 µU·mL⁻¹. By what factor does the glucagon-to-insulin ratio change?

options.text: 3 times higher
options.why: Right: 7.5 before, 22.5 after; 22.5 ÷ 7.5 = 3.

options.text: 2 times higher
options.why: This counts only the fall in insulin and ignores the rise in glucagon.

options.text: 1.5 times higher
options.why: This counts only the rise in glucagon and ignores the fall in insulin.

options.text: 3.5 times higher
options.why: This adds the two factors (1.5 + 2). Changes in a ratio multiply: 1.5 × 2 = 3.

variants.solution: Before: 90 ÷ 12 = 7.5. After: 135 ÷ 6 = 22.5. 22.5 ÷ 7.5 = 3. Or: glucagon × 1.5 and insulin ÷ 2 give 1.5 × 2 = 3.

variants.stem: In the last hour of an Ironman bike leg, a triathlete's glucagon rises from 70 to 210 pg·mL⁻¹ and insulin falls from 10 to 8 µU·mL⁻¹. By what factor does the glucagon-to-insulin ratio change?

options.text: 3.75 times higher
options.why: Right: 7 before, 26.25 after; 26.25 ÷ 7 = 3.75.

options.text: 3 times higher
options.why: This counts only the rise in glucagon and ignores the fall in insulin.

options.text: 4.25 times higher
options.why: This adds the two factors (3 + 1.25). Changes in a ratio multiply: 3 × 1.25 = 3.75.

options.text: 2.4 times higher
options.why: This divides the glucagon factor by the insulin factor (3 ÷ 1.25). A fall in insulin raises the ratio, so multiply.

variants.stem: Over a 25 km run, a runner's glucagon rises from 60 to 120 pg·mL⁻¹ and insulin falls from 9 to 3 µU·mL⁻¹. By what factor does the glucagon-to-insulin ratio change?

options.text: 6 times higher
options.why: Right: about 6.7 before, 40 after; 40 ÷ 6.67 = 6.

options.text: 3 times higher
options.why: This counts only the fall in insulin and ignores the rise in glucagon.

options.text: 5 times higher
options.why: This adds the two factors (2 + 3). Changes in a ratio multiply: 2 × 3 = 6.

options.text: 1.5 times higher
options.why: This divides the insulin factor by the glucagon factor (3 ÷ 2). A fall in insulin raises the ratio, so multiply.

variants.solution: Before: 60 ÷ 9 ≈ 6.67. After: 120 ÷ 3 = 40. 40 ÷ 6.67 = 6. Or: glucagon × 2 and insulin ÷ 3 give 2 × 3 = 6.

variants.stem: Insulin is low late in a long run, yet the runner's leg muscles take up more glucose than at rest. How?

options.text: Contraction moves GLUT4 to the membrane by its own signalling route
options.why: Right: Ca²⁺, AMPK and other contraction signals move GLUT4 independently of insulin.

options.text: Muscle becomes leaky, so glucose diffuses straight through the membrane
options.why: Glucose can't cross the fat layer of the membrane; it always needs a transporter such as GLUT4.

options.text: The little insulin that is left becomes ten times stronger
options.why: Exercise does improve insulin sensitivity afterwards, but during exercise the main route is contraction itself.

options.text: Glucagon moves GLUT4 into the muscle membrane
options.why: Glucagon acts mainly on the liver; muscle has few glucagon receptors.

variants.stem: A cyclist with type 1 diabetes injects his usual insulin dose, then rides hard for 2 h. Why is he at higher risk of low blood glucose than a rider without diabetes?

options.text: Injected insulin can't fall, so the liver stays braked
options.why: Right: the body can't switch the injected dose off, so the normal fall in insulin that frees liver glucose is missing.

options.text: His muscles can't take up any glucose without extra insulin
options.why: Contraction moves GLUT4 by its own route; the problem is too much insulin, not too little uptake.

options.text: His kidneys lose glucose into the urine during the ride
options.why: Glucose spills into urine only when blood glucose is very high, not low; his problem is too much insulin that can't be switched off.

options.text: Hard exercise destroys the insulin he has just injected
options.why: Exercise can speed insulin absorption from the injection site; it doesn't destroy it.

variants.stem: A triathlete eats a large sugary snack 45 min before a hard run, and her insulin is high when she starts. Some people then feel a glucose dip in the first 20 min. Why?

options.text: Insulin and contraction both pull glucose in; the liver is braked
options.why: Right: the two routes add up, and the liver is still braked by the high insulin.

options.text: The snack has already been used up before the run starts
options.why: Much of the glucose is still being absorbed or stored; the dip comes from faster uptake, not an empty gut.

options.text: Contraction stops insulin from working in the leg muscles
options.why: The opposite: contraction and insulin act by separate routes and their effects add together.

options.text: Running drops glucagon to zero in the first minutes
options.why: Glucagon doesn't vanish at the start; the dip is from extra uptake while insulin is still high.

variants.stem: A triathlete does two 30 min bike sessions on separate days: one at 40% VO₂max, one at 80%. What should you expect for blood cortisol?

options.text: No clear rise at 40%; a large rise at 80%
options.why: Right: in 30 min bouts, cortisol rose at 60% and 80% VO₂max but not at 40%.

options.text: A similar rise in both, as any exercise is a stress
options.why: Cortisol needs a hard enough effort; easy riding for 30 min didn't raise it.

options.text: A rise at 40% only; at 80% the ride is too short
options.why: The opposite: the harder session gave the bigger rise, even at the same length.

options.text: A rise in both, but only from plasma volume loss
options.why: Plasma volume loss adds a little, but at 80% ACTH also rose: the adrenal glands were releasing more.

variants.stem: Which session is most likely to give a runner the largest growth hormone response?

options.text: 20 min at a pace just above the lactate threshold
options.why: Right: at least 10 min above the lactate threshold appears to be the strongest endurance stimulus.

options.text: 60 min of easy jogging well below the threshold
options.why: Length alone isn't the main trigger; intensity above the lactate threshold matters most.

options.text: 5 min at a pace just above the lactate threshold
options.why: Right intensity, but likely too short: the review suggests at least 10 min.

options.text: 20 min of easy jogging below the threshold
options.why: Right length, but too easy: the response appears to need intensity above the lactate threshold.

variants.stem: A cycling coach says: "Adrenaline is what makes your liver pour out glucose when you ride." What is the best judgement?

options.text: Mostly wrong: glucagon and falling insulin drive it; adrenaline's role in very hard efforts is debated
options.why: Right: blocking adrenergic receptors hasn't reduced liver glucose output; the pancreatic hormones are in charge.

options.text: Right: adrenaline is the main driver of liver glucose output at all intensities
options.why: This was the long-held assumption; experiments that block its receptors haven't supported it.

options.text: Wrong: the liver releases no glucose during exercise
options.why: The liver's glucose output rises markedly in exercise; without it, blood glucose would crash.

options.text: Wrong: cortisol is the main driver within minutes
options.why: Cortisol acts over hours through genes; minute-to-minute control comes from glucagon and insulin.
